oil.summary: Crude markets ended June 30 in a split session: Brent edged up 0.83% to $73.76/bbl while WTI slipped 0.75% to $70.23/bbl, masking a brutal month that saw both benchmarks shed nearly 20%. The dominant narrative remains the Strait of Hormuz reopening, which is accelerating fears of a fresh supply glut — Morgan Stanley cut its Brent forecast to $75/bbl citing exactly that dynamic. Secretary Bessent's signal that the US may lift sanctions on Iranian oil stranded in tankers compounded the bearish pressure, with DD News reporting intraday declines of up to 3% on the headline. Refined products were hit harder: RBOB gasoline cratered 4.97% and heating oil fell 3.00% on the session. Asian refiners are redirecting recovered Persian Gulf cargoes to the US West Coast, though Asia's total crude imports remain well below pre-war levels. Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries add a minor offsetting supply risk.
drivers: Strait of Hormuz reopening accelerating supply glut fears; Morgan Stanley cuts Brent target to $75/bbl
Bessent signals possible removal of sanctions on Iranian oil in tankers, adding bearish supply expectations
Sharp refined-product sell-off (RBOB -4.97%, HO -3.00%) as Asian refiners redirect Middle East cargoes, pressuring crack spreads

gas.summary: Natural gas staged a notable recovery on both sides of the Atlantic today. Henry Hub surged 4.02% to $3.31/MMBtu, extending a strong weekly gain of 5.15%, while TTF climbed 2.61% to €43.675/MWh. The Hormuz corridor remains an active flashpoint for LNG flows, with Middle East producers reported to be pushing on with loadings despite ship attacks. Pakistan's emergency spot LNG purchase at a roughly $1/MMBtu premium to regional prices underscores near-term tightness in Asian markets. Longer-dated sentiment received support from Shell's forecast that global LNG demand will rise 65% by 2050, driven by South and Southeast Asian growth. ADNOC and Eni acquiring stakes in gas blocks tied to Argentina's LNG project adds upstream supply optionality on a multi-year horizon. Trump's public pressure on fuel retailers to cut pump prices adds political noise but limited fundamental impact.
drivers: Pakistan paying spot LNG premium signals near-term Asian tightness, supporting Henry Hub and TTF
Hormuz LNG flows continuing despite ship attacks, with supply disruption risk keeping prices bid
Shell's 65% LNG demand growth forecast to 2050 reinforces bullish structural backdrop

power.summary: EU carbon allowances (EUA) gained 2.08% to $76.41/EUA today, broadly consistent with TTF's 2.61% rise — higher gas prices lift the cost of coal-to-gas switching, supporting carbon prices. The month-to-date EUA gain of 2.19% contrasts with TTF's 5.06% monthly decline, suggesting carbon has found a near-term floor independent of gas. On the demand side, a new report identified the US as the leading driver of global CO2 emissions growth in 2025, accounting for roughly 30% of the increase — a politically sensitive data point as nuclear talks with Iran remain unresolved. A separate analysis warned that without $1.4 trillion in new US grid infrastructure, electricity prices could surge up to 58% by an unspecified future date, underscoring AI-driven power demand stress. The Hormuz crisis is credited with accelerating solar build-out across Southeast Asia, a structural shift with long-run implications for fossil fuel power demand in the region.
drivers: EUA up 2.08%, tracking TTF's gas price gain as higher gas costs support carbon's role in the switching stack
Report flagging US as top 2025 CO2 emissions growth driver adds regulatory risk premium to carbon outlook
Hormuz crisis cited as catalyst for Southeast Asian solar acceleration, signaling structural fossil-fuel demand erosion in the region
